newsitem.title: USA: Dole drops dot and World Wide Web wiggles.
newsitem.headline: Dole drops dot and World Wide Web wiggles.

text.p: For want of a dot, Bob Dole's campaign page got tangled in the World Wide Web -- and an Internet-savvy practical joker got more publicity than he bargained for.

The entanglement started at the end of Sunday's televised presidential debate, when Dole gave viewers his website address: "If you really want to get involved, just tap into my home page -- www.dolekemp96org."
The correct address is www.dolekemp96.org.
All Dole forgot was the second dot, but that was enough to shunt page-hunters aside. Many landed at what would have been plausible sites --- www.dole-kemp.org and www.dole-kemp.com.

But those sites were registered to Flying Penguin Productions Limited, a website design firm based in Arlington, Virginia. The firm's president, Ron Fitzherbert, had registered the sites the day before Dole announced Jack Kemp as his running mate, hoping to grab the campaign's attention and get a chance to pitch the firm's product.

The campaign call never came and the sites languished -- until Sunday's flub, that is. "For a little fun," Fitzherbert said in a statement, Flying Penguin rigged the sites with cryptic "click here" messages that transfered users to a Clinton-Gore campaign website at www.cg96.org.

Within 24 hours of the debate the Flying Penguin page got 70,000 hits, Fitzherbert said. He said he has cancelled the page registration, and users who call up the old page instead see his statement explaining the mix-up.

Dole was not the only malaprop on the campaign trail. President Clinton, using one of his standard lines about how race and ethnicity do not matter in the United States, managed to disavow the Constitution and the Bill of Rights instead.
Speaking at a night-time campaign rally Monday in Portland, Maine at a baseball stadium packed with 15,000 people -- his third speech in his third state that day -- Clinton got his lines crossed.

"In this country, it doesn't matter if you believe in the Constitution and the Bill of Rights and you're willing to show up tomorrow and be a good citizen -- everybody can have a place in America," Clinton said.
"And that's the way I want it to stay," he added.

Clinton attracted some Republican groupies, if not votes, while spending three days at the Chautauqua Institution, a retreat devoted to the arts and religion in a strongly Republican stretch of western New York state.
Taking a break from debate preparations, Clinton staged a brief photo-op Saturday morning, drawing scores of local residents out onto the retreat's central square.
One gray-haired man greeted another with some surprise: "What's a rock-ribbed Republican like you doing out here?"
The second, a touch embarrassed, pondered for a moment and replied: "It's the office, you know, it's the office."

The campaign trail can be a small world, as Dole discovered at the Tick Tock Diner in Clifton, New Jersey. He wound up sitting next to Linda Buel, who turned out to be the mother of the woman who serves Dole his morning coffee at a Washington cafe called Cuppa Cuppa.

Dole offered Buel a sheet of paper from an official Dole-Kemp notepad so she could write a note to her daughter, Jess. She wrote: "Dear Jess, My turn -- He's great. Just like you said. Love you, Mom."

Can Clinton predict the future? White House spokesman Mike McCurry apparently thought so, at least as regards Vice President Al Gore's performance in Wednesday night's televised debate with Republican counterpart Jack Kemp.
Seven hours before the vice presidential debate, McCurry told reporters that Clinton would offer a congratulatory call on Gore's excellent showing.
"The president will call him and ... congratulate him on his very strong performance," McCurry told reporters at his daily briefing shortly before 2 p.m. EDT.
The debate did not begin until 9 p.m. EDT.
